concept.name: Covariance
concept.definition: A measure of the joint variability of two random variables: the expected product of their deviations from their respective means. Its sign indicates the direction of the linear relationship (positive: variables tend to move together; negative: oppositely), and its magnitude depends on the units of the variables.
concept.intuition: It is the raw, unstandardized version of correlation: it tells you whether two variables move together and by how much in squared unit terms, but you cannot compare covariances across different unit scales.
concept.mechanics: For each paired observation, multiply the deviation of x from its mean by the deviation of y from its mean, then average these products. Normalizing covariance by the product of the standard deviations yields the Pearson correlation coefficient; in portfolio theory, asset covariances determine portfolio variance.
concept.formula: cov(X,Y) = E[(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y])] = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y]; sample estimate: q = SUM_{i=1..N}(x_i - x_bar)(y_i - y_bar) / (N - 1).
concept.failure_modes: Because covariance carries units of x times y, its magnitude is not comparable across variable pairs or scales - only its sign and the normalized correlation are interpretable. Zero covariance rules out linear dependence but not nonlinear dependence (e.g., X uniform on [-1,1] and Y = X^2 have covariance zero yet are perfectly dependent).
concept.misconceptions: Uncorrelated does not mean independent, except under joint normality. Also, a large absolute covariance does not by itself imply a strong relationship - it may just reflect large units or variances.
concept.example: If two stocks have daily returns with variances 0.0004 and 0.0009 and covariance 0.0003, their correlation is 0.0003 / sqrt(0.0004*0.0009) = 0.5; the covariance value alone says nothing without that normalization.
